notes.context: This networking assessment evaluates Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) and Reverse Path Broadcast (RPB), emphasizing their shared use of reverse unicast-path checks to prevent loops and duplicate packets. RPF applies to multicast: a router forwards an arriving packet only when it arrives on the interface used to reach the source via unicast routing; otherwise it discards the packet as a duplicate or invalid copy. RPB applies to broadcast: a node forwards the packet only along the appropriate outgoing link determined by the reverse unicast path, preventing broadcast loops and redundant transmissions. The assessment also covers RPF's role in IP spoofing prevention and the distinction between forwarding to multiple interfaces in RPF and selecting a suitable outgoing link in RPB.

notes.content: {"answer":"The purpose of Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) is the prevention of loops in a network when a multicast is sent from a node. It works in the way that each node has the knowledge about which node it would use for sending a unicast packet due to unicast routing algorithms. When a multicast packet arrives at a node’s entry port, the node would forward the packet to all other nodes (except for the one where the packet arrived) only if the node would also use this very node for sending the incoming packets to its source. Otherwise, the packet is discarded because it is most likely a duplicate. The purpose of Reverse Path Broadcast is to send a broadcast over the network without the occurrence of loops. It works in a similar way like RPF but here, a receiving node doesn’t forward the packet to all other nodes. A receiving node instead only forwards the packet to the node it would also send a unicast packet to.","manual_feedback":"The response correctly answers the purpose and the explanation for both broadcast types. RPF avoids loops not only in multicast but also in the broadcast.","manual_score":1.0,"question":"WHAT is the purpose of Reverse Path Forwarding and Reverse Path Broadcast? HOW do they work?"}
